analysis.one_liner: Lets the government import generic flu medicine made under compulsory licenses during a pandemic.
analysis.headline: The bill to allow imports of generic antiviral drugs for pandemic stockpiling was introduced in November 2005 and died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the United States import generic versions of patented drugs, such as the flu medicine Tamiflu, made under compulsory licenses — meaning the patent holder gets paid but other manufacturers can make the drug. At the time, the government had stockpiled enough antivirals to treat only 1-2% of the population, while health experts recommended enough for 25-40%. The bill would reverse a prior U.S. decision giving up the right to import such drugs under World Trade Organization rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans would gain a much larger emergency supply of pandemic medicine, at lower prices, because generics could be imported rather than waiting on a single foreign manufacturer's production capacity.

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes the President to import pharmaceutical products made under compulsory licenses to meet public health needs or to address inadequate supply caused by insufficient domestic manufacturing capacity [S2] [S3].

It directs the U.S. Trade Representative to declare the United States an 'eligible importing member' under the WTO's 2003 decision on the TRIPS Agreement and public health, and to withdraw the U.S. name from the list of countries that voluntarily gave up the right to import such drugs [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings note the government had stockpiled enough antivirals to treat only 1-2% of the population, while the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommended stockpiling enough for 25-40%, and that Roche, the sole Tamiflu rights holder, lacked U.S. manufacturing capacity to meet near-term needs [S3].
Imported drugs would still be subject to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, so they would face the same safety review as other medicines [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would lose some control over their patents during a public health emergency, receiving 'reasonable compensation' but facing generic competition. Taxpayers would fund the stockpile purchases, though likely at lower generic prices.

drawbacks.text: Compulsory licensing reduces patent holders' exclusive rights, which brand-name drug makers argue weakens the financial reward that funds development of new medicines — a cost supporters would have to acknowledge even in an emergency [S3].

The bill was a response to a single feared shortage (Tamiflu during a possible bird-flu pandemic); a broader compulsory-import authority could be invoked in ordinary supply disputes, not just true emergencies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine preparedness gap: the government had far less antiviral medicine on hand than public health experts recommended, and the sole patent holder could not quickly make enough. The trade-off — paying a patent holder less than full monopoly pricing during a declared emergency — is the standard mechanism WTO rules already allow for poorer countries. The main honest objection is that loosening patent exclusivity, even temporarily, could reduce incentives for future drug development.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen introduced the bill on November 18, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1] [S5].
Eleven members cosponsored the bill — 10 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
No further action was taken: there was no committee vote, no floor vote, and no action in the Senate before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies kept full control of their U.S. patents and monopoly pricing, and the government remained unable to import generic copies of patented drugs in a supply emergency. Americans got no new pandemic medicine supply from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Thomas H. Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents, and no Republican signed on, but the bill died quietly in committee rather than through a party-line vote.

industries.note: Compulsory-license imports would end their exclusive right to sell patented drugs like Tamiflu during a public health emergency, forcing them to accept 'reasonable compensation' instead of monopoly prices. Consumers would pay less and get more supply; the industry would earn less on the affected drugs.
The bill creates a lawful channel for generic versions of patented medicines to be made and imported to meet U.S. public health needs, expanding their market in emergencies.
